summary: Big Summit Prairie is a mostly private meadow in the Ochoco Mountains; no source we found describes a lookout tower on it.

access.note: Most of the prairie is privately owned and not open to the public. Forest Service roads 22 and 42 reach the edges and adjacent land (Oregon Encyclopedia).

evidence.supports: Prairie located in the Ochoco Mountains
evidence.quote: Located in the heart of the Ochoco Mountains, Big Summit Prairie is known for its diversity of wildflowers and birds.

evidence.supports: About thirty miles east of Prineville
evidence.quote: easily accessible from Prineville (thirty miles to the west)

evidence.supports: Name refers to its size; Little Summit Prairie about twelve miles east
evidence.quote: Big Summit Prairie received its name because of its size, which is larger than Little Summit Prairie, a smaller area twelve miles to the east.

evidence.supports: Settlers first claimed the prairie in the mid-1880s
evidence.quote: The Prairie was first homesteaded in the mid-1880s

evidence.supports: Settlers raised livestock as their main living
evidence.quote: Those who settled in the Prairie raised livestock as their primary livelihood.

evidence.supports: Hudspeth family bought the prairie in the 1950s for summer pasture
evidence.quote: The Hudspeth family purchased the entire Prairie in the 1950s and used it as summer pasture for their cattle.

evidence.supports: Most of the prairie is privately owned and inaccessible to the public today
evidence.quote: Today most of the Prairie is owned by Big Summit Prairies Inc. and Waibel Properties, LLC, and is inaccessible to the public.

evidence.supports: Forest Service roads 22 and 42 reach the edges and adjacent land
evidence.quote: U.S. Forest Service roads (22 and 42) provide access to the edges and adjacent lands

evidence.supports: Visitors come to see wildflowers and birds at the edges
evidence.quote: wildflower enthusiasts, birders, butterfly buffs, photographers, and sightseers

corrections.why: The Oregon Encyclopedia says most of the prairie is privately owned. Federal roads reach only its edges. The record may mean the prairie as a whole, or a lookout site on federal land; a human should check which.

notes_for_editor: No source read places a lookout on or near the prairie. The Oregon Lookouts entry gives only the county (Crook) and the Ochoco National Forest, with no description. The Crook County list on firelookout.org (NHLR and FFLOS data) has no Big Summit entry. The nearest lookouts seen were Black Mountain (an abandoned crow's nest on firelookout.org, described as a lookout platform in a 2011 trip report) and Mt. Pisgah (staffed, per the same 2011 trip report). Two searches and about five page reads found nothing else. Check whether this record is a lookout at all before the story is published. The story is short and covers the prairie, not a tower. Fact-check 2026-10-21: the story's sentence that the Oregon Encyclopedia article describes no lookout tower is a reading of the whole article (its only 'Lookout' hit is a reference title), not a quotable fact.
